focus: Exodus 4 completes the conversation at the bush as the LORD answers Moses’ remaining objections with signs, with His promise to be with his mouth, and with Aaron as his spokesman, then sends him back to Egypt. On the journey the LORD gives Moses His word for Pharaoh, confronts Moses over the circumcision of his son, and brings him to Aaron, and the chapter ends with Israel believing and worshiping.

sections.title: The LORD Gives Moses Signs for the People
sections.summary: When Moses fears that the people will not believe him, the LORD gives him three signs: the rod that becomes a serpent, the hand made leprous and restored, and water from the river that will become blood. These signs are given so “that they may believe that the LORD God of their fathers” (Exodus 4:5) has appeared to Moses.

sections.title: The Maker of Man’s Mouth Appoints Aaron as Spokesman
sections.summary: Moses pleads that he is slow of speech, and the LORD answers, “Who has made man’s mouth?” (Exodus 4:11), promising to be with his mouth. When Moses asks Him to send someone else, the LORD’s anger is kindled, yet He appoints Aaron as Moses’ spokesman and tells Moses to take the rod with which he will do the signs.

sections.title: Moses Returns to Egypt with God’s Word for Pharaoh
sections.summary: Jethro sends Moses away in peace, and Moses sets out for Egypt with his wife, his sons, and “the rod of God” (Exodus 4:20). The LORD tells him that He will harden Pharaoh’s heart and gives him the message, “Israel is My son, My firstborn” (Exodus 4:22), with the warning that Pharaoh’s own firstborn will die if he refuses to let God’s son go.

sections.title: The LORD Confronts Moses over His Son’s Circumcision
sections.summary: At the encampment on the way, “the LORD met him and sought to kill him” (Exodus 4:24). Zipporah circumcises their son, and the LORD lets Moses go.

sections.title: Aaron Meets Moses and the People Believe
sections.summary: The LORD sends Aaron to meet Moses at the mountain of God, and Moses tells him all the LORD’s words and signs. In Egypt Aaron speaks to the elders and the signs are done before the people, who believe and bow their heads in worship when they hear that the LORD has visited them.

1.brief: Moses objects that the people may not believe him or listen to him and may say, “The LORD has not appeared to you.” His fear now centers on whether Israel will accept him as God’s messenger.
1.explain:
“Then Moses answered and said, ‘But suppose they will not believe me or listen to my voice;”

Moses raised a third objection. “Suppose they will not believe me or listen to my voice.” God had already said, “they will heed your voice” (3:18), but Moses still doubted. His fear now centers on whether Israel will accept him as God’s messenger.

“suppose they say, ‘The LORD has not appeared to you.”

He imagined the people saying, “The LORD has not appeared to you.” Moses had no proof to show them. What would he say if they called him a liar or a dreamer?

2.brief: The LORD asks Moses, “What is that in your hand?” and Moses answers, “A rod.” God begins with the ordinary shepherd’s staff Moses already holds.
2.explain:
“So the LORD said to him, ‘What is that in your hand?”

The LORD answered with a question: “What is that in your hand?” God did not begin with something new. He began with what Moses already had.

“He said, ‘A rod.”

Moses answered, “A rod.” It was a shepherd’s staff, an ordinary tool for guiding sheep and leaning on while walking. God begins with the ordinary shepherd’s staff Moses already holds. Through it God would bring plagues on Egypt, part the sea, and bring water from the rock.
2.notes: The Hebrew word for “rod” refers to a staff or stick. Shepherds used such staffs to guide and protect their flocks.

3.brief: At the LORD’s command Moses throws the rod on the ground, it becomes a serpent, and Moses flees from it. The familiar staff becomes something Moses cannot control.
3.explain:
“And He said, ‘Cast it on the ground.”

God commanded, “Cast it on the ground.”

“So he cast it on the ground, and it became a serpent; and Moses fled from it.”

When Moses obeyed, “it became a serpent.” The staff turned into a snake. “Moses fled from it.” He was frightened. The familiar staff became something Moses could not control.
3.notes: The serpent was associated with royal power in Egypt and appeared on Pharaoh’s crown. The sign may have carried special meaning before Pharaoh, though Exodus does not draw that connection directly.

4.brief: The LORD tells Moses to take the serpent by the tail, and when he does, it becomes a rod again in his hand. Moses must trust God’s word enough to take hold of what frightened him.
4.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Reach out your hand and take it by the tail”

God gave a second command: “Reach out your hand and take it by the tail.” Anyone who handles snakes knows that grabbing a snake by the tail is dangerous, because it can turn and bite. God asked Moses to do the opposite of what instinct and experience would say.

“(and he reached out his hand and caught it, and it became a rod in his hand),”

Moses obeyed: “he reached out his hand and caught it.” When he did, “it became a rod in his hand.” Moses must trust God’s word enough to take hold of what frightened him. When he did, the danger became a tool in his hand again.

5.brief: The LORD explains that this sign is given “that they may believe that the LORD God of their fathers” has appeared to Moses. The miracle exists to confirm Moses’ message to the people.
5.explain:
“that they may believe that the LORD God of their fathers,”

God explained the purpose of the sign: “that they may believe.” The miracle was not for show. It was given so that Israel would believe that “the LORD God of their fathers” had sent Moses.

“the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.”

The people would know that the God of their fathers had truly appeared to Moses. The miracle exists to confirm Moses’ message to the people.
5.notes: This verse completes the sentence God began in 4:4, interrupted by the parenthesis describing what Moses did.

6.brief: The LORD tells Moses to put his hand in his bosom, and when he takes it out, it is leprous, “like snow.” The second sign shows God’s power over sickness and health in Moses’ own body.
6.explain:
“Furthermore the LORD said to him, ‘Now put your hand in your bosom.”

God gave a second sign. “Put your hand in your bosom.” The “bosom” was the fold of the robe at the chest.

“And he put his hand in his bosom, and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous, like snow.”

When Moses took his hand out, “his hand was leprous, like snow.” It was diseased, white and flaking. The second sign shows God’s power over sickness and health in Moses’ own body.
6.notes: The Hebrew word translated “leprous” covers a range of skin diseases and is not limited to the disease now called leprosy. “Like snow” most likely describes whiteness or flaking skin.

7.brief: When Moses puts his hand back in his bosom and draws it out, it is restored like the rest of his flesh. God who can afflict can also heal at once.
7.explain:
“And He said, ‘Put your hand in your bosom again.”

God said, “Put your hand in your bosom again.”

“So he put his hand in his bosom again, and drew it out of his bosom, and behold, it was restored like his other flesh.”

When Moses drew it out, “it was restored like his other flesh.” His hand was healed at once. God who can afflict can also heal at once.

8.brief: The LORD says that if the people do not believe Moses or heed the first sign, they may believe the message of the second. God gives a further sign for the people who are not persuaded by the first.
8.explain:
“Then it will be, if they do not believe you, nor heed the message of the first sign,”

God anticipated that some people might not be convinced by the first sign. Each sign carries a “message.” It speaks for God.

“that they may believe the message of the latter sign.”

The latter sign is the second sign. God gives a further sign for the people who are not persuaded by the first. He is patient with doubt.

9.brief: If they do not believe even these two signs, Moses is to pour water from the river on the dry ground, and it will become blood. The third sign looks ahead to the first plague on Egypt’s river.
9.explain:
“And it shall be, if they do not believe even these two signs, or listen to your voice,”

God provided for an even harder case: “if they do not believe even these two signs.”

“that you shall take water from the river and pour it on the dry land.”

Moses is to “take water from the river and pour it on the dry land.” The “river” is the Nile, the source of Egypt’s life.

“The water which you take from the river will become blood on the dry land.”

The water “will become blood on the dry land.” The third sign looks ahead to the first plague on Egypt’s river, when God would turn the Nile itself to blood (7:17–21). The river where Hebrew sons were drowned (1:22) would become a sign of judgment.

10.brief: Moses objects, “I am not eloquent,” saying he is slow of speech and slow of tongue. He turns from the people’s unbelief to his own weakness as a speaker.
10.explain:
“Then Moses said to the LORD, ‘O my Lord, I am not eloquent,”

Moses raised a fourth objection. “O my Lord, I am not eloquent.” He did not consider himself a skilled speaker. The phrase reads literally not a man of words.

“neither before nor since You have spoken to Your servant;”

This is Moses’ own claim about himself: he had never been eloquent, and even God’s speaking to him had not changed that. The narrative reports his assessment without confirming it.

“but I am slow of speech and slow of tongue.”

Moses may have meant that he struggled to find words, or that he spoke haltingly. The text does not say exactly what his difficulty was. He turns from the people’s unbelief to his own weakness as a speaker.
10.notes: Stephen describes Moses as “mighty in words and deeds” while in Egypt (Acts 7:22). Moses’ self-description here may reflect forty years away from Egyptian court life, a real speech difficulty, or simple reluctance. The text does not explain the difference.

11.brief: The LORD answers, “Who has made man’s mouth?” and reminds Moses that He is the One who makes people mute, deaf, seeing, or blind. Moses’ limitations are not beyond the Creator who made him.
11.explain:
“So the LORD said to him, ‘Who has made man’s mouth?”

The LORD answered with questions. “Who has made man’s mouth?” God made the human mouth. He is the Creator of speech.

“Or who makes the mute, the deaf, the seeing, or the blind?”

God is sovereign over every human ability and every human limitation.

“Have not I, the LORD?”

The answer is obvious. The God who made Moses’ mouth knows its weaknesses and can work through it. Moses’ limitations are not beyond the Creator who made him.

12.brief: The LORD commands Moses to go and promises, “I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall say.” The God who made the mouth will supply the words.
12.explain:
“Now therefore, go,”

God gave a direct command. The objections had been answered. It was time to obey.

“and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall say.”

With the command came a promise. The God who made the mouth will supply the words. Moses would not speak in his own strength.

13.brief: Moses pleads, “O my Lord, please send by the hand of whomever else You may send.” After every assurance, he asks God to send someone else.
13.explain:
“But he said, ‘O my Lord, please send by the hand of whomever else You may send.”

Moses’ fifth response was not an objection but a refusal. “Please send by the hand of whomever else You may send.” After every assurance, he asked God to send someone else.

His earlier questions expressed honest weakness. This request rejected a clear call. God had answered every objection. Moses simply did not want to go.

14.brief: The anger of the LORD is kindled against Moses, yet He names Aaron the Levite, Moses’ brother, who speaks well and is already coming to meet him gladly. God’s anger answers Moses’ refusal, but He still provides help for His servant.
14.explain:
“So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses,”

God had been patient with Moses’ questions, but He was angry at Moses’ refusal. God’s anger answers Moses’ refusal, but He still provides help for His servant.

“and He said: ‘Is not Aaron the Levite your brother? I know that he can speak well.”

God named a helper: “Aaron the Levite your brother.” Aaron was Moses’ older brother. God said, “I know that he can speak well.”

“And look, he is also coming out to meet you. When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.”

God had already set things in motion: “he is also coming out to meet you.” Before Moses agreed, God had prepared his help. “When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.” Aaron would welcome Moses gladly.
14.notes: Calling Aaron “the Levite” may point to his family line, which would later become the priestly tribe. Moses was also a Levite (2:1).

15.brief: Moses is to speak to Aaron and put the words in his mouth, and God promises to be with both their mouths and to teach them what to do. The message still comes from God through Moses, and Aaron serves within that commission.
15.explain:
“Now you shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth.”

God explained the arrangement. Moses would “speak to him and put the words in his mouth.” Moses would receive God’s message and give it to Aaron.

“And I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will teach you what you shall do.”

God repeated His promise and widened it: “I will be with your mouth and with his mouth.” God would help both brothers. He would “teach you what you shall do.” The message still comes from God through Moses, and Aaron serves within that commission.

16.brief: Aaron will be Moses’ spokesman to the people, a mouth for him, and Moses will be to him “as God.” The comparison describes their roles: Moses receives God’s word and Aaron speaks it.
16.explain:
“So he shall be your spokesman to the people.”

Aaron would speak for Moses.

“And he himself shall be as a mouth for you,”

Aaron “shall be as a mouth for you.” He would say what Moses gave him to say.

“and you shall be to him as God.”

Moses would relate to Aaron as God relates to a prophet, giving him the words to speak. The comparison describes their roles: Moses receives God’s word and Aaron speaks it. It does not mean that Moses was divine.
16.notes: Exodus 7:1 uses similar language: “I have made you as God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet.”

17.brief: Moses is to take the rod in his hand, with which he will do the signs. The rod from verse 2 becomes the instrument through which God will work before the people and Pharaoh.
17.explain:
“And you shall take this rod in your hand, with which you shall do the signs.”

God ended with a reminder about the rod. “You shall take this rod in your hand.” With it Moses would “do the signs.” The rod from 4:2 becomes the instrument through which God will work before the people and Pharaoh.

18.brief: Moses returns to Jethro his father-in-law and asks to go back to his brethren in Egypt to see whether they are still alive, and Jethro answers, “Go in peace.” Moses leaves Midian with his father-in-law’s blessing.
18.explain:
“So Moses went and returned to Jethro his father-in-law, and said to him,”

Moses “returned to Jethro his father-in-law.” He did not simply leave. He went to the head of the family he had joined.

“Please let me go and return to my brethren who are in Egypt, and see whether they are still alive.”

Moses asked permission: “Please let me go and return to my brethren who are in Egypt.” He gave a modest reason: to “see whether they are still alive.” He did not tell Jethro everything God had said.

“And Jethro said to Moses, ‘Go in peace.”

Jethro blessed him: “Go in peace.” Moses left Midian with his father-in-law’s blessing.

19.brief: The LORD tells Moses in Midian to return to Egypt, “for all the men who sought your life are dead.” God removes the danger that once drove Moses away.
19.explain:
“Now the LORD said to Moses in Midian, ‘Go, return to Egypt;”

The LORD spoke again “in Midian”: “Go, return to Egypt.”

“for all the men who sought your life are dead.”

God gave Moses reassurance. The Pharaoh who wanted to kill Moses had died (2:23). God removes the danger that once drove Moses away.
19.notes: The wording of this verse resembles Matthew 2:20, where an angel tells Joseph to return to Israel with the child Jesus, “for those who sought the young Child’s life are dead.”

20.brief: Moses sets his wife and sons on a donkey and returns to Egypt, carrying “the rod of God” in his hand. The shepherd’s staff is now named as God’s rod, marking Moses’ new mission.
20.explain:
“Then Moses took his wife and his sons and set them on a donkey, and he returned to the land of Egypt.”

Moses obeyed. He “took his wife and his sons and set them on a donkey.” He had at least two sons, Gershom (2:22) and Eliezer (18:4). The family set out for Egypt.

“And Moses took the rod of God in his hand.”

The staff is now called “the rod of God.” It is no longer just a shepherd’s tool. It belongs to God’s mission. The shepherd’s staff is now named as God’s rod, marking Moses’ new mission.

21.brief: The LORD tells Moses to do before Pharaoh all the wonders He has given him, but says, “I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go.” God prepares Moses for Pharaoh’s refusal and declares that He will be at work even in it.
21.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘When you go back to Egypt, see that you do all those wonders before Pharaoh which I have put in your hand.”

God gave Moses instructions for Egypt. “See that you do all those wonders before Pharaoh.” God had “put” these wonders “in your hand.” The power came from God.

“But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go.”

Then God warned Moses. God prepared Moses for Pharaoh’s refusal and declared that He would be at work even in it.

This is the first mention of hardening in Exodus. The story will show both sides. Pharaoh hardens his own heart (8:15, 32; 9:34), and God hardens it (9:12; 10:20). Pharaoh remains responsible for his refusal. He hears God’s command and rejects it again and again. God also carries out His own judgment and purpose through that refusal (9:16). The same sun that softens wax hardens clay. God’s pressure on a rebellious heart can harden it further as the person refuses to yield.
21.notes:
Several different Hebrew verbs are used for the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart in Exodus. The verb here means to make strong or firm.

Paul quotes 9:16 in Romans 9:17–18 in discussing God’s sovereign purposes.

22.brief: Moses is to tell Pharaoh that the LORD says, “Israel is My son, My firstborn.” Israel belongs to God as a son belongs to his father, which sets Pharaoh’s oppression against God’s own claim.
22.explain:
“Then you shall say to Pharaoh, ‘Thus says the LORD:”

Moses is to deliver God’s message to Pharaoh: “Thus says the LORD.” This is how prophets introduced a message from God.

“Israel is My son, My firstborn.”

This is God’s claim on Israel. Israel belongs to God as a son belongs to his father. The “firstborn” held a special place of honor and inheritance in the family. Israel belongs to God in a special way. Pharaoh’s oppression is set against God’s own claim.

Hosea later recalled this relationship: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, And out of Egypt I called My son” (Hosea 11:1). Matthew applies Hosea’s words to Jesus, God’s true Son, who was also brought out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15).

23.brief: God commands, “let My son go that he may serve Me,” and warns that if Pharaoh refuses, God will kill Pharaoh’s firstborn son. The demand aims at Israel’s worship of God, and the warning frames the final plague as justice for refusing God’s firstborn.
23.explain:
“So I say to you, let My son go that he may serve Me.”

God’s demand: “let My son go that he may serve Me.” The purpose of the release is worship. Israel was serving Pharaoh as slaves (1:13–14). God demands that His son be free to serve Him.

“But if you refuse to let him go, indeed I will kill your son, your firstborn.”

A warning follows. The demand aims at Israel’s worship of God, and the warning frames the final plague as justice for refusing God’s firstborn. Pharaoh had killed Israel’s sons (1:22). If he refused to release God’s firstborn, God would take Egypt’s firstborn. This warning is fulfilled in the tenth plague (12:29).

24.brief: On the way, at the encampment, “the LORD met him and sought to kill him.” The man sent to lead God’s people faces God’s deadly confrontation because he had not circumcised his son as God commanded Abraham’s descendants.
24.explain:
“And it came to pass on the way, at the encampment,”

A strange and difficult event follows. “On the way,” during the journey to Egypt, “at the encampment,” the place where the family stopped for the night.

“that the LORD met him and sought to kill him.”

The man sent to lead God’s people faced God’s deadly confrontation. The reason becomes clear in the next verse: Moses had not circumcised his son as God commanded Abraham’s descendants (Genesis 17:10–14). The form the threat took is not described, but it is best understood as a sudden, life-threatening illness.

God had just declared Israel His firstborn and warned of death for Pharaoh’s firstborn. Now God confronts Moses, whose own son lacked the sign of belonging to God’s people. The man sent to lead Israel under God’s covenant could not neglect it in his own home.
24.notes:
The Hebrew text says “him” without naming Moses, and interpreters have debated whether the LORD sought to kill Moses or his son. The setting and the ending (“So He let him go,” 4:26) are most naturally read as referring to Moses.

The reason for the delay is not recorded. Possibilities include a recent birth (perhaps of Eliezer, 18:4) with the eighth day falling on the journey, neglect while Moses was busy with the mission, or Moses giving in to Zipporah, who seems from her words in 4:25 to have resisted the practice. Scripture does not say which.

25.brief: Zipporah takes a sharp stone, circumcises her son, casts the foreskin at Moses’ feet, and says, “Surely you are a husband of blood to me!” Her quick action supplies the covenant sign that had been neglected in Moses’ household.
25.explain:
“Then Zipporah took a sharp stone and cut off the foreskin of her son”

“Zipporah took a sharp stone.” She acted quickly. She “cut off the foreskin of her son,” performing the circumcision herself. Flint knives were commonly used for circumcision (compare Joshua 5:2).

“and cast it at Moses’ feet,”

The Hebrew word for “feet” can be a polite way of speaking about the private parts. Either way, she presented the evidence that the covenant sign had been given.

“and said, ‘Surely you are a husband of blood to me!”

Her words are hard to interpret. They may express anger or distress at having to perform the rite. They may also acknowledge that through the shedding of blood, her husband’s life had been spared. Her quick action supplied the covenant sign that had been neglected in Moses’ household.
25.notes: The phrase “husband of blood” is difficult. It may reflect a connection between circumcision and marriage, or it may mean that Moses had been restored to her through blood. Interpreters have proposed several explanations, and none is certain.

26.brief: So the LORD lets Moses go, and Zipporah repeats, “You are a husband of blood!” because of the circumcision. The danger ends once the covenant sign is given, showing that God’s command matters even in the home of His chosen leader.
26.explain:
“So He let him go.”

The LORD released Moses. The danger ended once the covenant sign was given.

“Then she said, ‘You are a husband of blood!’—because of the circumcision.”

Zipporah says, “You are a husband of blood!” The narrator adds “because of the circumcision,” tying her words to what had just happened. The verse makes that link clear without settling whether she was speaking the words a second time.

The danger ended once the covenant sign was given, showing that God’s command matters even in the home of His chosen leader. God takes obedience seriously, even in what may seem a small command. He can discipline His own servants, and public calling does not excuse disobedience at home.
26.notes: Zipporah and the sons appear to have been sent back to Jethro at some point, for they rejoin Moses later in 18:2–6. The text does not say when or why.

27.brief: The LORD tells Aaron to go into the wilderness to meet Moses, and Aaron meets him at the mountain of God and kisses him. God brings the two brothers together at the very place where He called Moses.
27.explain:
“And the LORD said to Aaron, ‘Go into the wilderness to meet Moses.”

Meanwhile, in Egypt, the LORD was speaking to Aaron. God was directing both brothers. He had told Moses that Aaron was coming (4:14).

“So he went and met him on the mountain of God, and kissed him.”

Aaron “met him on the mountain of God,” Horeb, where God had called Moses (3:1). He “kissed him,” a warm greeting between brothers. God brings the two brothers together at the very place where He called Moses.

28.brief: Moses tells Aaron all the words of the LORD who sent him and all the signs He commanded. Aaron now knows the full message he is to speak.
28.explain:
“So Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD who had sent him,”

Moses “told Aaron all the words of the LORD.” He passed on everything God had said, as God had commanded (4:15).

“and all the signs which He had commanded him.”

He also told Aaron about the signs. Aaron now knew the full message he was to speak.

29.brief: Moses and Aaron go and gather all the elders of the children of Israel. They begin their mission with Israel’s leaders, as God had directed in Exodus 3:16.
29.explain:
“Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the children of Israel.”

Moses and Aaron arrived in Egypt and “gathered together all the elders of the children of Israel.” They began their mission with Israel’s leaders, as God had directed in 3:16.

30.brief: Aaron speaks all the words the LORD had spoken to Moses, and the signs are done in the sight of the people. God’s plan for Aaron to speak and for the signs to confirm the message is carried out.
30.explain:
“And Aaron spoke all the words which the LORD had spoken to Moses.”

“Aaron spoke all the words.” He served as spokesman, as God had arranged (4:16). He spoke “the words which the LORD had spoken to Moses.”

“Then he did the signs in the sight of the people.”

The signs confirmed the message. God’s plan for Aaron to speak and for the signs to confirm the message was carried out.
30.notes: The Hebrew text does not specify whether “he” who did the signs was Aaron or Moses. The nearest subject is Aaron, though God gave the signs to Moses (4:17).

31.brief: “So the people believed,” and when they hear that the LORD has visited them and seen their affliction, they bow their heads and worship. The chapter ends with Israel responding to God’s word with faith and worship.
31.explain:
“So the people believed;”

Moses had feared they would not believe him (4:1), but God had promised they would listen (3:18). God kept His word.

“and when they heard that the LORD had visited the children of Israel and that He had looked on their affliction,”

They “heard that the LORD had visited the children of Israel.” God had come to help them. He “had looked on their affliction.” The God who saw their suffering (2:25; 3:7) was acting.

“then they bowed their heads and worshiped.”

The people responded with worship. The chapter ends with Israel responding to God’s word with faith and worship. The goal God named in 3:12, that Israel would serve Him, has its first small beginning here, though the hardest days still lay ahead (5:20–21).
